books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, “A House Divided” speech, Springfield, Illinois, June 16, 1858. Public domain. Wording verified against the Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln (Miller Center transcript). Omissions between the quoted passages are marked.
stimulus.text: We are now far into the fifth year, since a policy was initiated, with the avowed object, and confident promise, of putting an end to slavery agitation. Under the operation of that policy, that agitation has not only, not ceased, but has constantly augmented. In my opinion, it will not cease, until a crisis shall have been reached, and passed — “A house divided against itself cannot stand.” I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free. . . . It will become all one thing, or all the other.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln’s claim that the government cannot endure “half slave and half free” most directly meant that

options.text: the Union would soon dissolve into two nations.
options.misconception: Lincoln says the opposite: “I do not expect the Union to be dissolved.”

options.text: the Union must become all free or all slave.
each state should decide slavery for itself alone.
options.misconception: Lincoln’s point is national: the whole Union must become one thing or the other.

options.text: Congress should ban slavery in the states at once.
options.misconception: Lincoln promises to block slavery’s spread, not to ban it where it already exists.

rationales.A: Lincoln says the opposite: “I do not expect the Union to be dissolved.”
rationales.B: “It will become all one thing, or all the other”: the house will cease to be divided, one way or the other.
rationales.C: Lincoln’s point is national: the whole Union must become one thing or the other.
rationales.D: Lincoln promises to block slavery’s spread, not to ban it where it already exists.
rationales.general:
1. Read Lincoln’s image: a house divided against itself cannot stand.
2. Read his claim: the government cannot endure permanently half slave and half free.
3. Read his forecast: it will become all one thing or all the other, free or slave.
4. Hear the warning: Lincoln was not predicting a war but a decision, and he meant the nation to choose freedom.
Remember: when a speaker says a house cannot stand divided, he is saying a choice is coming.
